item.title: What people in their 40s wish they'd known at 25
item.description: I was reading through some Reddit threads the other day — you know the ones, where people ask “what do you wish you’d known at 25?” — and I found myself nodding along to a lot of it. There’s something oddly comforting about reading advice from people who actually lived through the decade you’re currently in. Not theorists, not podcasters, just regular folks who figured some stuff out the hard way.

item.title: Book Publishing Process
item.description:
The stages of publishing a book, in rough order:

  1. Writing — research, drafting, revising until you have a complete manuscript.
  2. Editing — developmental editing for structure and narrative, then line editing for prose, then copyediting for grammar and consistency.
  3. Proofreading — final pass for typos and formatting errors before anything goes to print.
  4. Design — cover design and interior layout (fonts, margins, page breaks).
  5. Production — printing or e-book formatting. Offset lithography for large runs, digital printing for shorter ones.
  6. Marketing — promotional materials, advertising, media outreach, social media.
  7. Distribution — getting the book to readers via publishers, online retailers, bookshops, or direct sales.

Writing

Start with a concept, do the research, outline the structure, then draft. The first draft doesn’t need to be good — it needs to exist. Revision comes after. Get feedback from beta readers or a critique group before you consider the manuscript finished.

item.title: Bathukamma
item.description:
Bathukamma is a flower festival from Telangana. Women stack seasonal flowers into tiered arrangements, sing songs while dancing around them, and at the end of each day float them in water. It runs for about ten days in the autumn, usually September or October, and coincides with the end of the monsoon when flowers are at their peak.

The name comes from “Bathuku Amba” — may she live long — and is directed at Goddess Gauri. It’s not a festival with a single grand ceremony. It’s something that happens in neighbourhoods, courtyards, and public squares across Telangana, with each group making their own arrangement and singing their own songs.

item.title: The House That Bends
item.description:
Introduction to Maison Horta

Maison Horta is one of those buildings that makes you stop and stare. It’s on a quiet street in Brussels, tucked away behind what looks like an ordinary façade, but step inside and the whole thing opens up into something that feels almost impossible — a house made of curves, light, and ironwork that looks like it’s growing out of the walls.

Victor Horta built it in 1893, right at the tail end of what we now call Art Nouveau. The style is easy to recognise: flowing lines, organic shapes, a deliberate break from the stiff, symmetrical architecture that came before it. Horta didn’t just adopt the style — he helped invent it. Maison Horta is his first major work, and it’s still one of the best examples of what Art Nouveau could be.

item.title: The one thing that changed how I negotiate
item.description:
I used to think negotiation was about persuasion. About having the right words, the right tone, the right strategy. Turns out I was missing the whole point.

There’s a concept from negotiation theory called BATNA — Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement. It sounds academic, but it’s actually the single most practical thing you can know before walking into any discussion where two people want different things.

Your BATNA is what you’d actually do if the talks fall apart. Not what you hope for. Not what sounds good in your head. What you’d realistically do tomorrow morning when nothing has been agreed.

item.title: Affirmations that actually helped me
item.description:
I started doing affirmations roughly two years ago, after a particularly rough patch left me convinced I was fundamentally broken. Not in the dramatic sense – just that quiet, persistent voice in the back of my head telling me I wasn’t quite enough. You know the one.

The first time I tried it, I felt like an absolute idiot. Standing in front of the mirror, saying “I am worthy” out loud, while my brain screamed bullshit. I lasted about forty-five seconds before giving up.

item.title: How I stopped participating in gossip
item.description:
I used to gossip. Not the dramatic, scheming kind — just the everyday variety. The “can you believe what so-and-so did” chatter that happens in offices, group chats, and among friends. It felt harmless enough. Social bonding, right?

Then I realised something uncomfortable: the people who gossip the most are usually the same people who will gossip about you the moment you leave the room. Once I noticed that pattern, I couldn’t unsee it. And honestly, it made me tired.

item.title: Reducing negativity in personal and professional life
item.description:
Some things that help keep negativity at bay:

  • Notice when you’re spiralling. Naming the pattern breaks it.
  • Set boundaries with people who consistently drain you.
  • Limit social media. Curate your feeds so they’re not just outrage and comparison.
  • Take walks. Physical movement changes mental state.
  • Keep a gratitude list. Three things a day is enough.
  • Learn to say no without over-explaining.
  • Don’t participate in gossip. Change the subject or leave the room.
  • Forgive yourself for mistakes. You’ll make more of them.
  • Get enough sleep. Everything feels worse when you’re tired.
  • Do one thing well each day instead of doing ten things poorly.
  • Journal when your head is noisy. Getting thoughts out of your head and onto paper helps.
  • Surround yourself with people who challenge you constructively, not ones who just agree with everything.
  • Accept that some things are out of your control. Focus on what you can influence.
  • Take breaks. Regular ones, not just when you’re burning out.
  • Declutter your workspace. Physical mess feeds mental mess.

item.title: A list of emotions I keep coming back to
item.description:
I started keeping a list of emotions because I realised I didn’t have names for half the things I was feeling. Not clinical names — just everyday words that would let me say “I’m feeling X” instead of “I don’t know what’s wrong but something is.”

It sounds simple, but most people never build that vocabulary. We grow up with maybe twenty or thirty emotion words and then we just reuse them forever. Happy, sad, angry, stressed. That’s it. When something more specific comes up — like the particular flavour of disappointment you get when someone forgets your birthday but you pretend it didn’t matter — you don’t have a word for it. So you just sit with it, unnamed, and it gets heavier.

item.title: How to make a vision board (that you'll actually use)
item.description:
I’ve tried vision boards before. Like most people, I made a nice collage, pinned it somewhere visible, and then promptly forgot it existed. The problem wasn’t the board — it was that I never actually sat down and thought about what I wanted. I just pasted random pictures of beaches and sports cars and called it a day.

This time I wanted to do it properly. Not the Pinterest aesthetic kind, but the kind where you actually force yourself to decide what matters across different areas of your life. So I built a markdown template instead. It’s simpler, it lives in my notes, and it forces structure onto the chaos.

item.title: What is a vision board
item.description:
A vision board is a collage of images and words that represent what you want to achieve. The idea is that seeing your goals visually keeps them in focus and motivates action.

You can make one physically with printed images and a pinboard, or digitally with tools like Canva or Pinterest. It works for short-term targets as well as longer aspirations.

Sources:

  • Oxford Dictionaries: http://www.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/vision_board
  • Psychology Today: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/click-here-happiness/202103/what-is-vision-board-and-why-make-one

item.title: Inner child therapy
item.description:
Inner child therapy works from the idea that parts of us retain the emotions, memories, and needs from childhood. If those needs went unmet, they can shape how we think and behave as adults.

The therapy aims to identify those old wounds, give them space to be expressed, and respond to them with the compassion they didn’t receive originally. Techniques include guided imagery, journaling, letter writing to your younger self, and dialogue exercises.

item.title: Memento Mori
item.description:
Memento Mori – remember you must die. The oldest trick in the Stoic toolbox, and still the one that cuts deepest when you actually let it land.

It’s not meant to be morbid. The point isn’t to sit around thinking about corpses, it’s to use the fact of your mortality as a filter for what actually matters. You could leave life right now – not today necessarily, but at some point, and probably sooner than you think. Knowing that changes the weight of things. Most of the stuff you’re worrying about right now will not matter in a year, let alone at the end. That’s not depressing, it’s liberating.

item.title: Amor Fati
item.description:
Amor fati – love of one’s fate. Nietzsche’s phrase for the attitude that everything that happens to you, including the awful bits, is not just bearable but necessary, and ideally something you can welcome rather than merely endure.

I keep coming back to it because it’s the harder half of the Stoic pair. Memento Mori tells you to remember you will die, which is useful for cutting through nonsense. Amor Fati tells you to love what happens to you, which is useful for not going mad while it’s happening. One without the other feels incomplete – mortality without fate is just anxiety, and fate without mortality is just fatalism.

item.title: A bit of madness goes a long way
item.description:
You don’t have to be crazy to live on Earth. But to some it helps to be.

I saw this somewhere and it stuck because it is quietly true in a way that has nothing to do with clinical anything and everything to do with the simple fact that normal is a setting on a washing machine, not a lifestyle. The people who get anywhere – not necessarily successfully, just somewhere worth being – are the ones who are slightly unhinged about something. Obsessed in a way that makes other people uncomfortable. Willing to look foolish because the alternative is looking exactly like everyone else and going exactly where everyone else is going.

item.title: No good deed ever goes unpunished
item.description:
“No good deed ever goes unpunished.”

I’ve said this more times than I care to admit, usually in the aftermath of trying to help someone and ending up with more problems than I started with.

It’s a peculiar thing – the people you’d expect to be grateful are often the ones who punish you most for trying. I think about my parents sometimes, how every time I offer to sort something out or take on a burden, it somehow spirals into getting used. The intention is never in doubt but the outcome always ends up feeling used.

item.title: The advantages you've had
item.description:
“Whenever you feel like criticizing any one, just remember that all the people in this world haven’t had the advantages that you’ve had.”

– F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby

I read this somewhere and it stuck with me because it’s true in a way that feels obvious until you actually try to live by it, and even then it’s hard. We all have advantages we never asked for and rarely notice – the kind of things that just make life slightly easier, like being born into a family that didn’t struggle to put food on the table, or having parents who went to university and could help you with homework without feeling lost themselves, or arriving in a country where you speak the language and look like most of the people around you. None of these things were earned. They just happened. And they add up in ways that are impossible to quantify but impossible to ignore.

item.title: Some notes on digital content strategy
item.description:
I came across a set of notes on digital content strategy and thought I’d share the bits that stuck with me. Nothing earth-shattering, but useful if you’re trying to think more clearly about how content actually works across platforms.

QR codes

They’re everywhere now. Easy enough to scan, instant redirect to a page or product. Fine as a bridge between the physical and digital world, though I’m not convinced they’ve earned their place in most campaigns yet.

item.title: Staying Online
item.description:
Back in the ’80s the Bee Gees crooned “Staying Alive.” In today’s parlance, that would be “Staying Online.”

Corny reference aside, the point is: building a web presence is one of the most important things you can do for your personal and professional life. But what does that actually mean? Is it just getting an email address? Putting up a website? Something about your online conduct? It’s all of those things and more. It’s closer to creating an identity — the online version of who you are.

item.title: Iomega Customer Service in India
item.description:
A few months back I picked up a Prestige portable hard drive from IT dot COM, a shop in Margao, Goa. It worked fine for a while, then one day the indicator light started blinking and wouldn’t stop. The drive wouldn’t show up on any of the computers I plugged it into.

I was in Hyderabad at the time. I looked up authorised Iomega service centres nearby and found none. None in Hyderabad, none in Secunderabad. So I waited till I was back in Goa and took the drive to the store.

item.title: An Email from Weebly
item.description:
Got this email from Weebly after a week of inactivity. It’s genuinely good writing – playful without being annoying:

It’s been 7 days, 4 hours, 13 minutes and 2 seconds since you last logged in, and we’re starting to get really worried.

We were just getting to know each other. You created 1 site, 1 page, dragged on 1 element, and then… nothing.

We were really excited for your new website, it had so much potential!

item.title: Slash vs Backslash
item.description:
A thread on Hacker News about the eternal confusion between / and :

jordanlund: Confession time… I always get confused about which one is the slash and which one is the backslash. I end up calling them “the one on the question mark” and “the one not on the question mark”.

zem: Here’s a simple trick: \ leans back, / leans forward.

grantrules: _ is a slash that got tired and lay down.

item.title: Road Construction in Goa
item.description:
I commute from Margao to Bambolim every day. Normally a 30-minute drive. Today it took me an hour and forty minutes.

There’s road construction near Verna that started four days ago. Four days of digging with no visible progress. And they’ve decided the best time to work is during peak hours – 9:30 am to late evening. Exactly when everyone is trying to get to or from work.

I was late for an important meeting today. Had to apologise to my boss and to clients. All because someone thought it was a good idea to block a major route during rush hour.

item.title: What Is Education? Is College Worth It?
item.description:
Everyone tells you to go to college. It’s the default path. Finish school, get a degree, find a job.

But is it actually worth it? The tuition costs are rising, graduates are struggling to find work in their field, and student debt is becoming a genuine burden.

For some people, college is absolutely the right choice. The networking, the structured learning, the credential – it all adds up. For others, it’s four years and a mountain of debt for a piece of paper that doesn’t open any doors.

item.title: Lemonlaw
item.description: Sat at CCD today with friends and we ended up looking up people on Lemonlaw. It only took five minutes. I know that’s not the point of the thing, but it felt wrong how easy it was.

item.title: Too Much Change?
item.description:
A friend mentioned recently that we’re going through too many changes. I didn’t really know what to make of it at the time, but it stuck with me.

Later that day I did something daft — I reverted my Facebook profile picture to an old one. I knew it was pointless as soon as I did it. Changing a profile picture doesn’t anchor anything. But I think I was reaching for something familiar, something that hadn’t changed, even if it was just an image on a screen.
